topics.title: Neuron and activation
topics.description: A neuron combines weighted inputs and a bias, then applies a nonlinear activation; without nonlinearity, stacked layers remain a linear transformation.

lessons.title: Combine inputs
lessons.body: A neuron first multiplies each input by its weight, adds the results, and adds a bias. For two inputs this value is z = w1*x1 + w2*x2 + b. The weights and bias are parameters learned during training.

lessons.title: Interpret weights and bias
lessons.body: A positive weight makes an increase in its input increase the weighted sum when the other inputs are held fixed; a negative weight makes it decrease. The bias shifts the sum independently of the inputs. These are local statements about this calculation, not a guarantee of how an entire network behaves.

lessons.title: Apply an activation
lessons.body: The activation transforms the weighted sum into the neuron's output. ReLU, for example, returns max(0, z): it outputs zero for a negative z and z itself when z is positive. Other activation functions have different shapes and may be chosen for different layers or tasks.

lessons.title: Work through an example
lessons.body: Suppose x1 = 2, x2 = 1, w1 = 0.5, w2 = -1, and b = 0.25. The weighted sum is 0.5*2 - 1*1 + 0.25 = 0.25, so ReLU returns 0.25. If the bias were -0.5 instead, the sum would be -0.5 and ReLU would return zero.

lessons.title: Why nonlinearity matters
lessons.body: Without nonlinear activations, a stack of dense layers with weighted sums and biases can be combined into one affine transformation. Nonlinear activations allow the network to represent more complex relationships. They do not guarantee that training will succeed or that the learned pattern will generalize.

topics.title: Layers and representations
topics.description: Each layer transforms an input into a representation for later layers; useful representations depend on the training objective and data.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: A layer transforms its input into values passed to the next layer. Those values form a representation: a way of encoding information that later computations can use. The representation is learned from data through the training objective rather than manually assigned a meaning.

lessons.title: Follow the transformations
lessons.body: For an image classifier, an input image is converted to numbers and passed through successive layers before the final layer produces class scores. Intermediate layers can emphasize different patterns. Their precise behavior depends on the architecture, data, and learned parameters; the values in the illustration are schematic.

lessons.title: Track shapes
lessons.body: The output shape of one layer must be compatible with the input expected by the next. For example, a dense layer producing a vector of 16 values can feed a layer that expects 16 inputs. A shape mismatch is an implementation error, not evidence that the learned representation is poor.

lessons.title: Understand the objective
lessons.body: Training adjusts the network to reduce a specified loss on training examples. A representation useful for classifying images is not automatically suitable for a different task or population. Evaluate it on the intended task and representative held-out data.

lessons.title: Avoid overinterpreting
lessons.body: A hidden value does not necessarily correspond to one human-readable concept, and a pattern may be spread across many values. Visualization or probing can help investigate a representation, but an appealing picture alone does not establish how the network makes every decision.

topics.title: Weights and biases
topics.description: Weights scale input contributions and biases shift activations; training updates both to reduce a specified loss.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: For a neuron with inputs x1 and x2, the pre-activation value is z = w1*x1 + w2*x2 + b. The weights w1 and w2 scale the inputs, while bias b shifts the sum. An activation then transforms z into the neuron's output.

lessons.title: Read their effect
lessons.body: Holding other inputs fixed, a positive weight makes the pre-activation sum rise as its input rises; a negative weight makes it fall. Bias adds the same offset regardless of that input. Later nonlinearities and layers can make the complete network's behavior more complex.

lessons.title: Calculate an example
lessons.body: If x1 = 2, x2 = 1, w1 = 0.5, w2 = -1, and b = 0.25, the sum is 0.25. Changing b to -0.5 changes the sum to -0.5. With ReLU, the resulting outputs are 0.25 and 0 respectively.

lessons.title: Update parameters
lessons.body: During training, an optimizer uses gradients of a specified loss to adjust weights and biases. For gradient descent, each update subtracts a learning-rate-scaled gradient from a parameter. A single update need not improve performance on every example.

lessons.title: Check generalization
lessons.body: A low training loss does not guarantee that the learned parameters work on new examples. Compare performance on representative held-out data and investigate errors relevant to the task. Avoid treating an individual weight as a complete explanation of a network's prediction.

topics.title: Forward pass
topics.description: A forward pass computes outputs by applying layer operations in sequence, making tensor shapes and transformations auditable.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: A forward pass computes a network's output from its input using the current parameter values. Each layer transforms the result of the previous layer; during training, the output can then be compared with a target to compute a loss.

lessons.title: Apply a layer
lessons.body: For a scalar input x = 2, weight w = 3, and bias b = -1, an affine layer computes z = w * x + b = 5. A following ReLU activation returns max(0, z), so this layer's activated output is 5.

lessons.title: Follow shapes
lessons.body: Suppose a batch contains four examples, each with three features. Multiplying a 4-by-3 input matrix by a 3-by-2 weight matrix yields a 4-by-2 result before adding a compatible bias. Keeping the dimensions explicit helps catch invalid operations.

lessons.title: Interpret the output
lessons.body: The last layer's output depends on the task and model design. A regression network may output a number; a classifier may output logits that require a suitable conversion before being interpreted as probabilities. Check the actual output contract.

lessons.title: Separate forward and learning
lessons.body: A forward pass alone does not update weights. In training, a loss is computed from the output, gradients are calculated, and an optimizer applies updates. In evaluation, parameters generally remain fixed while predictions are measured on held-out data.

topics.title: Loss function
topics.description: A loss measures prediction error and defines the signal training optimizes; it should match the task and output representation.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: A loss function measures how a model's prediction compares with a target. During training, the optimizer uses gradients of the loss to update parameters. Choose a loss that fits the task and the model's output.

lessons.title: Regression example
lessons.body: For numeric prediction, squared error is the square of prediction minus target. If a model predicts 7 and the target is 5, the squared error is 4. Mean squared error averages such errors across examples.

lessons.title: Classification example
lessons.body: For classification, cross-entropy can penalize a model that assigns low probability to the correct class. Libraries differ in whether a loss expects probabilities or raw logits, so check the function's contract to avoid applying a transformation twice.

lessons.title: Loss and metrics
lessons.body: The training loss is not always the same as the metric used to judge the product. For example, classification training may use cross-entropy while evaluation tracks precision and recall. Choose metrics that reflect the costs of errors.

lessons.title: Monitor generalization
lessons.body: Track loss on training and held-out validation data. A decreasing training loss alongside worsening validation loss can indicate overfitting, though data or measurement issues can also contribute. Investigate before selecting a response.

topics.title: Gradient descent
topics.description: Gradient descent updates parameters using loss gradients, and the learning rate controls the step size.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Gradient descent adjusts model parameters to reduce a loss. The gradient describes how the loss changes locally with the parameters; an update moves opposite the gradient, scaled by a learning rate.

lessons.title: Calculate an update
lessons.body: For a parameter value of 2, gradient of 0.5, and learning rate of 0.1, a plain gradient-descent step gives 2 - 0.1 * 0.5 = 1.95. Actual neural networks update many parameters together.

lessons.title: Choose a learning rate
lessons.body: A very large learning rate can cause unstable updates, while a very small one can make progress slow. The useful range depends on the model, data, and optimizer. A schedule can change the rate during training.

lessons.title: Use batches
lessons.body: Mini-batch gradient descent computes an update from a subset of training examples. Different batches can produce different gradient estimates. Batch size affects memory, update frequency, and training behavior.

lessons.title: Monitor progress
lessons.body: Track training loss and a separate validation metric. If training is unstable or progress stalls, inspect learning rate, data, and gradients before changing settings. Lower training loss alone does not establish good generalization.

topics.title: Backpropagation
topics.description: Backpropagation applies the chain rule to calculate parameter gradients efficiently from the output layer toward earlier layers.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Backpropagation uses the chain rule to calculate how a loss changes with model parameters. It moves gradient information backward through the computations used in the forward pass.

lessons.title: Compute the forward pass
lessons.body: The model transforms inputs through its layers to produce a prediction. A loss function compares that prediction with the target. Intermediate values are needed to calculate gradients during the backward pass.

lessons.title: Apply the chain rule
lessons.body: If a quantity depends on an intermediate value, its derivative with respect to an earlier value combines derivatives along the path. Backpropagation reuses these local derivatives rather than separately recomputing the full derivative for every parameter.

lessons.title: Update parameters
lessons.body: After gradients are computed, an optimizer uses them to update parameters. Backpropagation calculates the gradients; the optimizer determines the update using its learning rate and other settings.

lessons.title: Check gradients
lessons.body: Inspect loss and gradient behavior during training, and compare a small calculation with a numerical gradient when debugging custom operations. Vanishing, exploding, or incorrect gradients can prevent effective learning.

topics.title: Training batches
topics.description: A batch supplies examples for an optimizer update; batch size changes memory use, gradient noise, and update frequency.

lessons.title: What a batch does
lessons.body: A training batch is a group of examples processed together to calculate a loss and gradients. An optimizer then uses those gradients to update model parameters. A data pass, or epoch, typically contains multiple batches, with a possible smaller final batch. The exact update schedule depends on the training loop.

lessons.title: Batch size and memory
lessons.body: Larger batches usually require more memory for inputs and intermediate activations. They can improve hardware utilization, but the result depends on the model, device, and implementation. If a batch does not fit, a smaller batch is one option; gradient accumulation is another when implemented with the intended loss scaling. Measure actual memory and throughput rather than assuming a larger batch is always faster.

lessons.title: Gradient estimates
lessons.body: A mini-batch gradient estimates a training signal from a subset of examples. Different batches can produce different gradients, so batch size changes the noise in that estimate as well as how often updates occur. Larger batches do not guarantee better generalization, and changes in batch size can require retuning the learning rate or schedule. Compare outcomes under a controlled experiment.

lessons.title: Shuffle without leaking
lessons.body: For many independent examples, shuffling training data helps prevent batches from reflecting an arbitrary file order. Do not mix held-out validation or test rows into training batches. Some tasks require different handling: time-ordered or sequence data may need order preserved within an example, and a split must still respect time or group boundaries. Follow the requirements of the data and model.

lessons.title: Count updates carefully
lessons.body: With 100 training examples and batch size 20, a single pass contains five batches if all examples are used once. If each batch produces one optimizer update, that is five updates per epoch. Gradient accumulation, dropping an incomplete final batch, or distributed training can change the count. Record the actual update schedule when comparing experiments.

topics.title: Epochs and iterations
topics.description: An epoch passes through the training set once, while an iteration is one optimizer update; they are not interchangeable.

lessons.title: Distinguish a pass from an update
lessons.body: An epoch is one pass through the training dataset. An iteration usually means one optimizer update, although some tools use it for a batch-processing step. State the convention in training logs: processing a batch and updating parameters are separate operations when gradients are accumulated.

lessons.title: Count batches in an epoch
lessons.body: With 100 examples and batches of 20, an epoch contains five batches. If the optimizer updates after each batch, three epochs produce 15 updates. When the dataset size is not divisible by the batch size, keeping or dropping the last incomplete batch changes this count.

lessons.title: Account for gradient accumulation
lessons.body: Suppose an epoch contains 12 microbatches and gradients are accumulated over three microbatches before each optimizer step. That gives four updates per epoch, not 12. Clear gradients at the intended update boundary and specify what happens to a partial accumulation group at the end.

lessons.title: Read the schedule's clock
lessons.body: A learning-rate scheduler may advance per epoch or per optimizer update. Calling a per-epoch scheduler after every batch makes it progress too quickly. When changing batch size, record both examples processed and optimizer steps so comparisons reveal whether the model received a different training budget.

topics.title: Training and validation curves
topics.description: Comparing training and validation loss helps reveal underfitting and overfitting when validation data is not used to fit weights.

lessons.title: Measure on separate data
lessons.body: Training loss measures fit to examples used to update weights. Validation loss measures the current model on separate examples without updating it. Plot both against epochs or optimizer steps using consistent loss definitions; the validation set guides model choices rather than supplying training gradients.

lessons.title: Read a widening gap
lessons.body: Suppose training loss falls from 0.8 to 0.2 while validation loss falls to 0.5 and then rises to 0.7. The later training fits training-specific patterns more closely without improving validation performance. Save checkpoints so the earlier, better-validating model remains available.

lessons.title: Investigate two high losses
lessons.body: If both curves stay high, inspect whether the model can learn even a small training subset. Incorrect labels, badly scaled inputs, a disconnected gradient, or an unsuitable learning rate can prevent fitting. A curve alone cannot distinguish those causes from insufficient model capacity.

lessons.title: Compare like-for-like measurements
lessons.body: Dropout, data augmentation, and regularization penalties can make the logged training loss differ from validation loss even without overfitting. Evaluate a training subset in evaluation mode with the same loss definition to clarify the comparison. Treat the observed trend as evidence to investigate, not an automatic diagnosis.

topics.title: Classification heads
topics.description: A softmax head normalizes logits for mutually exclusive classes but does not guarantee that its probabilities are calibrated.

lessons.title: Produce class scores
lessons.body: A classification head maps the network's final representation to class scores called logits. For a batch of eight examples and three mutually exclusive classes, the output can have shape 8-by-3. Each row describes one example, and each column must correspond to the same class throughout training and serving.

lessons.title: Convert logits to probabilities
lessons.body: Softmax exponentiates each logit and divides by the sum of those exponentials. Logits [0, 0] therefore give probabilities [0.5, 0.5]. Implementations subtract the largest logit first for numerical stability. Many cross-entropy functions already include this calculation and expect raw logits as input.

lessons.title: Separate exclusive and overlapping labels
lessons.body: An animal photo assigned exactly one species fits a softmax head. A photo that can independently contain a dog, a bicycle, and a person needs multiple labels, often modeled with one sigmoid output per label. Those probabilities need not sum to one; use a compatible binary loss for each label.

lessons.title: Choose a decision rule
lessons.body: Selecting the largest softmax probability yields a class, but a product may instead abstain below a confidence threshold. Set that policy using validation data and the cost of errors. A probability of 0.9 is not automatically calibrated: check how often predictions with similar confidence are actually correct.

topics.title: Regression heads
topics.description: A regression output and loss should reflect the target's scale, range, and error costs.

lessons.title: Output a numeric target
lessons.body: A regression head predicts quantities rather than class membership. A single unconstrained linear output can represent a temperature above or below zero. For several targets, use several outputs and keep their order and units explicit; a predicted price and a predicted duration are not interchangeable columns.

lessons.title: Match the loss to error costs
lessons.body: For a target of 5 and prediction of 7, absolute error is 2 and squared error is 4. Squared error puts more emphasis on large misses than absolute error. Select a loss based on the task rather than choosing an output activation intended for classification.

lessons.title: Respect ranges and scaling
lessons.body: An unconstrained output can predict a negative duration. A positive-valued transformation such as softplus can enforce positivity when that matches the target. If training uses standardized targets, save the training mean and scale and invert the transformation before reporting predictions in the original units.

lessons.title: Inspect errors beyond the mean
lessons.body: A low overall mean absolute error can hide systematic underprediction for large targets. Plot prediction errors against target size and report errors in the units users need. A point prediction alone gives no uncertainty interval; estimating intervals requires an additional method and held-out coverage checks.

topics.title: Overfitting
topics.description: Overfitting occurs when a network learns training-specific details that do not generalize to relevant unseen examples.

lessons.title: Recognize memorization
lessons.body: A neural network can fit accidental patterns or mislabeled examples in its training set. Overfitting appears when those improvements fail to transfer to relevant unseen data. Parameter count alone does not establish whether a model overfits; the amount and quality of data and the training procedure also matter.

lessons.title: Compare error trajectories
lessons.body: If training accuracy rises from 85% to 99% while validation accuracy stalls near 83%, additional training has not demonstrated better generalization. Inspect validation loss too: confidence can become worse even when the predicted class stays unchanged. Keep a checkpoint from before the deterioration.

lessons.title: Check the split before regularizing
lessons.body: Near-duplicate images or records from the same subject in training and validation can hide overfitting. Split by the independent unit relevant to deployment, such as a person or device. A suspiciously small gap can reflect leakage rather than excellent generalization.

lessons.title: Change one remedy at a time
lessons.body: More representative data, label-preserving augmentation, weight decay, dropout, or earlier stopping may reduce overfitting. Compare a chosen change on the same validation split instead of applying every remedy together. If training performance is already poor, stronger regularization may make the problem worse.

topics.title: Compute and memory
topics.description: Parameters, activations, gradients, and optimizer state use memory; estimate the full training footprint before selecting batch size.

lessons.title: Count persistent training state
lessons.body: Training needs storage for parameters, their gradients, and optimizer state. A million FP32 parameters occupy about four million bytes for the parameters alone. Gradients and two FP32 moment buffers add about twelve million more bytes, before activations, temporary buffers, or framework overhead.

lessons.title: Account for activations
lessons.body: Intermediate activations are often retained for the backward pass. Increasing batch size or input resolution can therefore raise memory usage even when parameter count is unchanged. For sequence models, longer inputs can also increase attention memory sharply. Measure peak usage during a full training step, not just model loading.

lessons.title: Distinguish memory from speed
lessons.body: A model that fits on a device can still train slowly because of data loading, small operations, or communication. Measure examples processed per second after warmup and inspect where time is spent. Reducing parameters does not guarantee faster execution if activations or inefficient kernels dominate.

lessons.title: Fit a run to the device
lessons.body: If a full training step runs out of memory, try a smaller microbatch and measure again. Gradient accumulation can preserve the effective batch size across several microbatches, but batch-dependent operations may behave differently. Leave headroom for variable input sizes and checkpoint or evaluation work.

topics.title: Neural-network baselines
topics.description: A small neural network or non-neural baseline gives a reference for judging whether added depth is worthwhile.

lessons.title: Establish a reference prediction
lessons.body: A baseline makes a neural network's result interpretable. For numeric prediction, a constant training-set mean is a useful starting point under squared error. For classification, predicting the most frequent training class exposes how much accuracy is possible without learning input-dependent patterns.

lessons.title: Train a small model first
lessons.body: A linear predictor or small multilayer perceptron can reveal whether the features contain usable signal before a larger network consumes the budget. Use the same split and preprocessing rules as the larger candidate. Record training time and inference cost along with the task metric.

lessons.title: Make the comparison fair
lessons.body: Suppose a deep model reaches 92% accuracy and a small network reaches 91.8%. Repeat runs or quantify uncertainty before attributing the difference to depth. Different data versions, tuning budgets, or thresholds can explain a small apparent gain even when the reported metric is identical.

lessons.title: Keep or reject added complexity
lessons.body: Prefer the larger model only when its measured benefit justifies the extra latency, memory, or maintenance. Inspect important error groups rather than deciding from the aggregate score alone. Preserve the baseline artifact as a reference for later regressions and data changes.

topics.title: Initialization
topics.description: Variance-aware initialization preserves useful activation and gradient scales better than setting all weights to zero.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Initialization chooses the starting values of a network's parameters before training. Starting values affect the scale of activations and gradients, which can make optimization easier or harder.

lessons.title: Break symmetry
lessons.body: If identical neurons in the same layer start with identical weights and biases and receive identical gradients, they remain identical under the same updates. Randomly initializing weights differently helps neurons learn different features. Biases may still be initialized to zero.

lessons.title: Control scale
lessons.body: Weights that are too large can make activations or gradients grow, while weights that are too small can make signals shrink across layers. Variance-aware schemes select an initialization scale using layer dimensions and assumptions about the activation.

lessons.title: Match the activation
lessons.body: Xavier initialization is commonly used with tanh-like activations, while He initialization is commonly used with ReLU-like activations. These are starting choices, not guarantees: architecture, normalization, data, and implementation details also matter.

lessons.title: Check early training
lessons.body: Inspect activation and gradient distributions and watch the loss in early batches. If signals vanish, explode, or become non-finite, investigate initialization alongside input scaling, learning rate, and the rest of the model. Compare candidate setups on the intended task.

topics.title: Learning-rate schedules
topics.description: Schedules adjust step size over training to balance rapid early learning with stable convergence.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: A learning-rate schedule changes an optimizer's learning rate during training according to a chosen rule. The learning rate affects update size; a schedule is a training choice, not a guarantee of better convergence.

lessons.title: Reduce over time
lessons.body: A step schedule lowers the rate at specified milestones. A smooth schedule may decrease it gradually. For example, a rate could drop from 0.01 to 0.001 after a chosen epoch; the appropriate values depend on the optimizer, model, and data.

lessons.title: Understand warmup
lessons.body: Warmup starts with a smaller learning rate and increases it over an initial period before the main schedule. It can help stabilize some training setups, especially when early updates are sensitive. It is not required for every model.

lessons.title: Track the schedule
lessons.body: Record the rate at each optimizer step or epoch and check the intended units. If a scheduler expects steps but is advanced once per epoch, it follows a different curve than planned. When resuming training, restore scheduler state together with model and optimizer state.

lessons.title: Compare fairly
lessons.body: Compare schedules with the same data split, training budget, and evaluation metric. Watch for divergence, slow learning, and held-out performance; a lower training loss does not necessarily mean better generalization. Repeat runs when randomness could materially change the result.

topics.title: Momentum and adaptive optimizers
topics.description: Momentum smooths updates and adaptive optimizers scale them using gradient history; neither removes the need to tune and validate.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: An optimizer uses gradients to update model parameters. Momentum and adaptive optimizers incorporate gradient history, but their behavior depends on settings and the training problem.

lessons.title: Understand momentum
lessons.body: Momentum maintains a running direction informed by recent gradients. Consistent gradients can accumulate in that direction, while changing directions can be smoothed. The update also depends on the learning rate and the momentum coefficient.

lessons.title: Understand adaptive scaling
lessons.body: Adaptive methods use statistics of past gradients to scale parameter updates. Adam, for example, tracks moving averages of gradients and squared gradients with bias correction. The resulting effective step size can vary across parameters.

lessons.title: Tune and compare
lessons.body: Compare optimizers using the same data split, metric, and training budget. Tune learning rate and other relevant settings for each rather than comparing default settings alone. Faster initial loss reduction does not guarantee better held-out performance.

lessons.title: Monitor training
lessons.body: Track training and validation metrics and investigate instability or stalled progress. Check learning-rate schedules, gradient magnitudes, and preprocessing before changing methods. Save optimizer state when resuming so its accumulated statistics are not accidentally discarded.

topics.title: Weight decay
topics.description: Weight decay discourages large weights to regularize a model; decoupled weight decay is not identical to L2 penalties for every optimizer.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Weight decay is a regularization technique that shrinks selected parameter values during optimization. It can help control model complexity, but its effect depends on the optimizer, parameter groups, and chosen strength.

lessons.title: Understand shrinkage
lessons.body: A decoupled weight-decay update applies a shrinkage term separately from the loss gradient update. Larger decay can shrink weights more strongly, but too much can harm learning. The exact update depends on the optimizer implementation.

lessons.title: Distinguish L2 penalties
lessons.body: An L2 penalty adds a parameter-size term to the loss. For plain gradient descent it can correspond to an appropriate weight-decay update, but with adaptive optimizers the penalty gradient is scaled by the optimizer, so it is not generally equivalent to decoupled decay.

lessons.title: Choose parameter groups
lessons.body: Some training setups exclude bias or normalization parameters from decay, while others use different policies. Follow the model and optimizer's conventions and record which parameters receive decay rather than assuming every parameter is treated the same way.

lessons.title: Tune on validation data
lessons.body: Compare decay strengths with an appropriate validation metric and a controlled training setup. Monitor both underfitting and overfitting. Weight decay is not a guarantee of better generalization and does not replace good data or evaluation.

topics.title: Dropout
topics.description: Dropout masks activations during training as regularization and should be disabled for ordinary inference.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Dropout randomly masks selected activations during training as a form of regularization. It can reduce reliance on particular activations, but its effect depends on where and how strongly it is applied.

lessons.title: Apply the mask
lessons.body: For each training pass, a dropout layer samples which activations to keep according to its configured probability. Common inverted-dropout implementations scale retained activations during training so ordinary inference does not need the same random masking.

lessons.title: Switch to evaluation mode
lessons.body: For ordinary deterministic inference, put the model in evaluation mode so dropout is disabled. Other layers can also behave differently between training and evaluation. Intentional Monte Carlo dropout is a separate technique with different requirements.

lessons.title: Tune the rate
lessons.body: Too much dropout can make fitting difficult, while too little may have limited regularization effect. Compare rates and placement using validation data under a controlled setup. The best setting is task-dependent.

lessons.title: Check behavior
lessons.body: Test that repeated ordinary inference calls use evaluation mode and monitor validation quality. Save and restore relevant training state when reproducibility matters. Dropout does not replace a representative test set.

topics.title: Batch normalization
topics.description: Batch normalization uses minibatch statistics during training and stored running statistics at inference.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Batch normalization normalizes activations using statistics and usually includes learned scale and shift parameters. Its behavior differs between training and ordinary evaluation in common implementations.

lessons.title: Use batch statistics
lessons.body: During training, a batch-normalization layer commonly computes a mean and variance from the current minibatch and updates running estimates. The exact dimensions and update rules depend on the layer and framework.

lessons.title: Switch to evaluation mode
lessons.body: With running-statistics tracking enabled, ordinary evaluation commonly uses the stored estimates instead of the current batch statistics. Check the framework configuration: disabling tracking or using a different normalization layer changes behavior.

lessons.title: Consider batch size
lessons.body: Small or unrepresentative batches can produce noisy statistics. Batch composition and distributed training configuration can also affect the estimates. Compare alternatives when the batch setup makes the usual statistics unsuitable.

lessons.title: Validate and save state
lessons.body: Save the layer's running statistics with the model and test that inference uses the intended mode. Compare validation behavior across representative batches. Correct tensor shapes do not ensure that training and serving normalization agree.

topics.title: Layer normalization
topics.description: Layer normalization normalizes features within each example, making it useful when batch sizes or sequence lengths vary.

lessons.title: Normalize within an example
lessons.body: Layer normalization rescales a selected set of features within each example using their mean and variance. In many sequence models, it is applied to the feature vector at each token position, though the normalized dimensions depend on the implementation. It does not require statistics from other examples in the batch. This differs from normalization that uses batch-level statistics.

lessons.title: Compute the normalization
lessons.body: For a feature vector, subtract its mean and divide by the square root of its variance plus a small epsilon. Epsilon helps avoid division by zero or unstable division when variance is very small. For features [1, 3], the mean is 2 and the population variance is 1, so the normalized values are approximately [-1, 1] when epsilon is small. Actual results depend on the chosen dimensions and epsilon.

lessons.title: Learn scale and shift
lessons.body: Layer normalization commonly includes learnable scale and shift parameters, often called gamma and beta. After normalization, the layer multiplies by gamma and adds beta for the configured features. These parameters let the model learn useful output scales and offsets. They are trained with the rest of the model rather than calculated as batch statistics.

lessons.title: Compare with batch normalization
lessons.body: Layer normalization typically computes statistics within each example over configured features. Batch normalization commonly uses batch statistics during training and stored running statistics during evaluation, depending on configuration. These choices behave differently when batch composition or size changes. Select a method based on architecture and data rather than assuming that either method is universally better.

lessons.title: Test dimensions and behavior
lessons.body: Check which axes are normalized in the library implementation and whether scale and shift are enabled. Verify tensor shapes for both training and inference, especially when sequence lengths or padding vary. Layer normalization is not a substitute for masking padded tokens in attention or losses. Compare model behavior with a baseline rather than assuming normalization guarantees training success.

topics.title: Convolutions
topics.description: Convolutions reuse local filters across positions and exploit spatial locality in images and other grid-like inputs.

lessons.title: Reuse a local filter
lessons.body: A convolutional layer applies the same learned filter at many spatial positions. A 3-by-3 filter looks at a local patch rather than connecting independently to every image pixel. Sharing weights lets the layer detect a pattern at different locations with fewer parameters than a comparable dense mapping.

lessons.title: Calculate an output shape
lessons.body: With a 5-by-5 input, a 3-by-3 kernel, stride 1, no padding, and dilation 1, each spatial output dimension is 3. Padding by one pixel on each side instead preserves the 5-by-5 size. Stride controls how far the filter moves between output positions.

lessons.title: Combine channels
lessons.body: For an RGB input, one standard convolutional filter spans all three input channels. A layer with eight 3-by-3 filters has 3*3*3*8 = 216 kernel weights and produces eight output channels, plus eight biases if enabled. Spatial weight sharing keeps that count independent of image width.

lessons.title: Understand the spatial assumption
lessons.body: Convolutions are useful when nearby positions have related meaning, as pixels often do. Arbitrarily ordered table columns do not necessarily have that property. Padding creates boundary effects, and stride can change the response to small translations, so test the shifts and edge cases expected in real inputs.

topics.title: Pooling and downsampling
topics.description: Downsampling reduces spatial compute but can discard fine details needed for localization or small-object recognition.

lessons.title: Reduce spatial resolution
lessons.body: Pooling summarizes a neighborhood without learning a separate weight for each position. Max pooling retains the largest value; average pooling retains the mean. Downsampling reduces spatial dimensions and later computation, but discards information that may be needed to distinguish small objects or precise boundaries.

lessons.title: Work through a pooling window
lessons.body: For the 2-by-2 patch [[1, 3], [2, 0]], max pooling returns 3 and average pooling returns 1.5. A 2-by-2 window with stride 2 maps a 4-by-4 feature map to 2-by-2 when no padding is used. Each output summarizes a different non-overlapping patch.

lessons.title: Compare learned downsampling
lessons.body: A strided convolution downsamples while learning how to combine local values; pooling uses a fixed reduction rule. Neither guarantees preservation of all useful details. Rapid spatial variation can alias when sampled more coarsely, so filtering before subsampling may help when small input shifts cause unstable outputs.

lessons.title: Preserve detail when the task needs it
lessons.body: Image classification can often use global average pooling to turn each feature map into one value. Segmentation needs a spatial output, so architectures may retain high-resolution features or pass them through skip connections to a decoder. Evaluate small-object and boundary errors before increasing downsampling.

topics.title: Embeddings
topics.description: Embeddings map discrete identifiers to learned vectors whose geometry reflects the training objective, not universal similarity.

lessons.title: Look up a learned vector
lessons.body: An embedding table stores one trainable vector per discrete identifier, such as a token or product ID. Looking up an ID retrieves its row. Unlike using the raw ID as a number, this representation does not imply that product 20 is twice product 10.

lessons.title: Size the table
lessons.body: A vocabulary of 1,000 identifiers with 16-dimensional embeddings requires 16,000 parameters. Looking up a batch of four sequences of length six produces a 4-by-6-by-16 tensor. The downstream model decides how to combine those vectors into predictions.

lessons.title: Learn similarity from the objective
lessons.body: Training gradients update embedding rows according to the task. Two items may become close because users interact with both, not because they share every semantic property. Cosine similarity reflects that learned geometry; it is not proof of universal meaning or interchangeability.

lessons.title: Handle unknown and rare IDs
lessons.body: Reserve a documented unknown-ID strategy for values absent from training and give padding its own treatment. Rare IDs receive fewer learning signals, so examine their errors separately. Save the ID-to-row mapping with the embedding weights; changing the mapping silently assigns vectors to the wrong inputs.

topics.title: Padding and masks
topics.description: Padding equalizes sequence lengths; attention and loss masks must prevent padded positions from affecting learning.

lessons.title: Build a rectangular batch
lessons.body: Sequences of lengths three and five can share a batch by adding two padding positions to the shorter one. The resulting tensor has length five for both examples. Padding is a storage convention, not real content, so later calculations must know which positions are valid.

lessons.title: Mask attention and loss separately
lessons.body: An attention mask prevents real tokens from attending to padded key positions. A loss mask excludes padded target positions from the training objective. One does not automatically implement the other. A causal mask adds a different restriction: a position cannot attend to later tokens.

lessons.title: Normalize over valid tokens
lessons.body: Suppose a batch contains eight real target tokens and two padding positions. Sum the losses on the eight valid tokens and divide by eight for a token-average loss. Dividing by all ten positions makes the reported value depend on how much padding happens to be in the batch.

lessons.title: Test padding invariance
lessons.body: In evaluation mode, append padding while preserving the original real-token positions and compare outputs for those tokens within numerical tolerance. Unexpected changes can expose a missing mask or incorrect pooling denominator. Confirm mask conventions in the library, since a true value can mean either allowed or blocked.

topics.title: Class imbalance
topics.description: Class weighting or sampling can emphasize rare examples but may change the probability calibration of the resulting classifier.

lessons.title: Expose the majority-class shortcut
lessons.body: If only 1% of examples are positive, predicting negative for everything gives 99% accuracy and zero positive recall. Inspect class counts and a confusion matrix before judging a classifier. Use metrics and operating thresholds that reflect the cost of missing positives and raising false alarms.

lessons.title: Reweight or resample training examples
lessons.body: Class-weighted loss increases the contribution of selected classes. Oversampling instead presents some examples more often, while undersampling discards some majority examples. Both change training emphasis, but repeated rare examples can still be memorized. Apply sampling only to training data, not the held-out evaluation population.

lessons.title: Separate ranking from probability quality
lessons.body: A classifier trained on an artificially balanced sample does not automatically output probabilities appropriate for a population with 1% positives. Evaluate calibration on representative held-out data before treating its scores as risks. Threshold adjustment and probability calibration address different questions.

lessons.title: Measure a usable operating point
lessons.body: If a review team can inspect 50 alerts daily, measure how many true positives occur among those alerts and how many positives are missed. Report the positive sample count and uncertainty. A large recall change based on two additional cases may not be stable enough to support a release.

topics.title: Data augmentation
topics.description: Augmentations encode label-preserving variation and should match plausible conditions in the deployment environment.

lessons.title: Encode a valid invariance
lessons.body: Data augmentation changes a training input while preserving the intended target, or transforms the target consistently. A small brightness change may preserve an image's species label. Rotating a digit can change its identity, so a transformation valid for one task may be wrong for another.

lessons.title: Transform labels with inputs
lessons.body: When horizontally flipping an image for object detection, flip the bounding boxes too. For a box with horizontal coordinates x_min and x_max in a width-W image, the flipped coordinates are W-x_max and W-x_min under a continuous edge-coordinate convention. Inspect transformed examples to verify the annotation convention.

lessons.title: Separate training variation from evaluation
lessons.body: Apply random augmentation to the training partition after splitting. Otherwise, transformed copies of one original can leak across partitions. Validation normally uses a fixed preprocessing path; if using test-time augmentation, define the transformations and aggregation explicitly and include their inference cost.

lessons.title: Choose realistic strength
lessons.body: Compare a modest augmentation policy with no augmentation on the same validation set. Inspect failures caused by crops that remove the object or distortions stronger than deployment conditions. More variation can hurt when it erases the signal the model must learn.

topics.title: Early stopping
topics.description: Early stopping chooses a checkpoint using validation behavior and should not repeatedly adapt to a held-out test set.

lessons.title: Stop on validation behavior
lessons.body: Early stopping ends training when a chosen validation metric stops improving. It limits training time and can reduce overfitting. Choose whether the metric should rise or fall before training; lower validation loss is better, while a metric such as recall usually has the opposite direction.

lessons.title: Track patience and minimum improvement
lessons.body: Suppose validation loss reaches 0.40, then measures 0.41, 0.405, and 0.42. With patience of three evaluations and no required minimum decrease, those are three consecutive non-improvements. Patience is counted at validation checks, which may occur more or less often than once per epoch.

lessons.title: Restore the selected checkpoint
lessons.body: The last training weights need not be the best validation weights. Save a checkpoint whenever the monitored metric improves and reload that checkpoint before the final test. If training may resume, preserve optimizer and scheduler state too; weights alone are sufficient only for some inference uses.

lessons.title: Avoid selecting on the test set
lessons.body: Use validation data to choose patience and the stopping checkpoint. Repeatedly examining test performance after each epoch makes the test influence selection. A noisy or unrepresentative validation set can also choose a poor checkpoint, so inspect its coverage rather than assuming stopping always improves generalization.

topics.title: Transfer learning
topics.description: Pretrained representations can reduce data needs, but domain mismatch determines how well they transfer.

lessons.title: Reuse a pretrained representation
lessons.body: A pretrained network supplies weights learned on a source task. For a new classifier, replace its original output head with one matching the target classes. Reusing the earlier layers can reduce labeled-data needs, but the benefit depends on how well source representations fit the new domain.

lessons.title: Start with frozen features
lessons.body: Freeze the pretrained backbone and train the new head first. This provides a relatively cheap reference and avoids immediately changing every pretrained weight. Frozen parameters do not necessarily freeze running statistics in normalization layers; choose training and evaluation modes deliberately.

lessons.title: Unfreeze selectively
lessons.body: If frozen features are insufficient, unfreeze later blocks or the full backbone and compare validation performance. A smaller backbone learning rate can limit abrupt changes to pretrained representations. Verify that newly trainable parameters are included in the optimizer when changing which layers are frozen.

lessons.title: Check the source assumptions
lessons.body: Preserve the expected channel order, input normalization, and tokenizer or image-processing contract. Evaluate target-domain slices, especially those unlike the pretraining data. Compare with the frozen reference so extra fine-tuning cost is justified by a measured improvement rather than assumed transfer.

topics.title: Residual connections
topics.description: Residual paths give gradients and representations a shortcut through deep blocks, often improving optimization.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: A residual block combines a transformed input with a shortcut: y = F(x) + x when the shapes match. The block learns the residual transformation F rather than requiring the entire mapping to pass only through that transformation.

lessons.title: Trace the forward path
lessons.body: The input x follows two paths: one passes through F, and the other is carried along the shortcut. Their outputs are added element by element. If F(x) is zero, the block's output equals x, although actual blocks may include other operations such as normalization or activation.

lessons.title: Trace gradients
lessons.body: For the simple sum y = F(x) + x, the derivative with respect to x contains both the derivative through F and an identity contribution from the shortcut. This gives gradients a direct path through the addition, often helping optimize deep networks. It does not guarantee that gradients or training will always be stable.

lessons.title: Match shapes
lessons.body: Elementwise addition requires compatible shapes. If a block changes the number of channels or spatial dimensions, the shortcut may use a projection or downsampling so it matches F(x). Check the architecture's exact operations rather than assuming every shortcut is an identity.

lessons.title: Validate the design
lessons.body: Compare a residual design with an appropriate baseline using the same data and evaluation protocol. Track training behavior, held-out performance, and inference cost. A shortcut can improve optimization without guaranteeing better accuracy for every task.

topics.title: Attention
topics.description: Attention combines value vectors using query-key compatibility and masks to control which positions can interact.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Attention constructs an output for a query by weighting value vectors according to compatibility between that query and corresponding keys. The weights depend on the input, so different queries can combine information differently.

lessons.title: Compute attention weights
lessons.body: In scaled dot-product attention, each query is compared with keys using dot products scaled by the square root of key dimension. A softmax over eligible keys converts scores into nonnegative weights that sum to one for that query.

lessons.title: Combine values
lessons.body: Multiply each value vector by its attention weight and sum the results. For scalar values 10 and 20 with weights 0.25 and 0.75, the output is 17.5. The weights describe this combination, not a complete explanation of the model's decision.

lessons.title: Apply masks
lessons.body: A causal mask prevents a position from attending to later positions in an autoregressive sequence. A padding mask prevents padded positions from contributing. The exact mask depends on the task and implementation; every query needs a valid set of eligible keys.

lessons.title: Check shapes and costs
lessons.body: For a sequence of n queries and m keys, the score matrix has n rows and m columns per attention head. Full attention across a long sequence can be expensive in memory and compute. Test any approximation or context limit against the task rather than assuming it is lossless.

topics.title: Transformer blocks
topics.description: Transformer blocks combine attention, feed-forward layers, normalization, and residual paths; ordering changes model behavior.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: A transformer block combines attention and a position-wise feed-forward network with residual connections and normalization. Variants differ in how these operations are ordered and in which attention masks they use.

lessons.title: Mix context with attention
lessons.body: Self-attention lets a token representation use information from allowed positions in the sequence. A causal mask prevents a position from attending to later positions, while other tasks may allow different attention patterns.

lessons.title: Transform each position
lessons.body: The feed-forward sublayer applies a learned nonlinear transformation to each position's representation. It typically shares the same parameters across positions. Attention mixes information across positions; the feed-forward sublayer transforms each resulting representation.

lessons.title: Connect and normalize
lessons.body: Residual paths add a sublayer's input to its output, with compatible dimensions. Layer normalization is placed before or after a sublayer depending on the architecture. These choices affect training behavior, so follow the specific model's design.

lessons.title: Check shapes and masks
lessons.body: Track batch, sequence, and hidden dimensions through the block, and verify that the mask matches the task. Test padding and causal behavior with small examples. A shape-compatible block can still be wrong if it exposes future information.

topics.title: Recurrent networks
topics.description: Recurrent networks reuse hidden state across sequence steps but can struggle to preserve long-range gradients.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: A recurrent neural network processes a sequence one step at a time, updating a hidden state from the current input and previous state. The state summarizes information useful to the model's task.

lessons.title: Follow a sequence
lessons.body: At each position, the network combines the current input with the previous hidden state to compute a new state. It may produce an output at every step or use a later state for a sequence-level prediction.

lessons.title: Train through time
lessons.body: Backpropagation through time computes gradients across the unrolled sequence. Repeated operations can make gradients shrink or grow over long spans, making learning difficult. Truncating the backward span also limits which earlier dependencies receive gradient signal.

lessons.title: Use gated variants
lessons.body: LSTM and GRU architectures use gates to control information flow through state. Gates can help with longer dependencies, but they do not guarantee that all long-range information will be retained. Compare architectures on the actual task.

lessons.title: Handle sequence boundaries
lessons.body: Reset or carry state according to the application's sequence boundaries, and mask padding where needed. Test variable-length inputs and prevent information from one independent sequence leaking into another through unintended state reuse.

topics.title: Encoder-decoder models
topics.description: Encoder-decoder systems transform an input sequence into an output sequence, often using autoregressive decoding.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: An encoder-decoder model maps an input sequence to an output sequence. The encoder builds representations of the input, and the decoder uses them to generate the output.

lessons.title: Encode the input
lessons.body: The encoder processes the source sequence into representations that carry information for the task. Padding masks and input preprocessing must match the model's design so padding is not treated as ordinary content.

lessons.title: Decode sequentially
lessons.body: An autoregressive decoder generates each output token using earlier output tokens and the encoded source. During generation, its own previous outputs become context; an early mistake can influence later tokens.

lessons.title: Connect source and output
lessons.body: Cross-attention lets a decoder position use encoder representations when the architecture supports it. Decoder self-attention and cross-attention have different inputs and masks. Other encoder-decoder architectures connect the components differently.

lessons.title: Evaluate generation
lessons.body: Test complete outputs on representative held-out examples with task-relevant metrics and human inspection where useful. Check length limits, stopping behavior, and whether outputs preserve important source information.

topics.title: Multi-task learning
topics.description: Shared representations can help related tasks but can also create negative transfer when task gradients conflict.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Multi-task learning trains a model on more than one task, often sharing part of its representation while using task-specific outputs. Related tasks can share useful signals, but sharing does not always help.

lessons.title: Structure shared learning
lessons.body: A shared encoder can feed separate prediction heads, each trained against its own target. Data availability and labels may differ by task, so the training procedure must handle missing labels appropriately.

lessons.title: Balance objectives
lessons.body: A combined loss can weight each task's loss. The weights and scales influence the shared update, so one task can dominate if its contribution is much larger. Choose weights using the goals and evaluation for the actual tasks.

lessons.title: Identify negative transfer
lessons.body: Sharing can hurt a task if the shared representation or updates favor another objective. Compare each task with a suitable single-task baseline and inspect per-task outcomes; an improved aggregate can hide a regression.

lessons.title: Evaluate and monitor
lessons.body: Use task-appropriate held-out metrics and representative data for each task. Check performance across relevant groups and monitor changes after deployment. Adjust task weighting or sharing only after investigating the evidence.

topics.title: Fine-tuning strategies
topics.description: Full and parameter-efficient tuning trade adaptation capacity against compute, memory, and preservation of pretrained behavior.

lessons.title: Choose what to update
lessons.body: Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model to a task by training on task-specific data. Full fine-tuning updates all selected model parameters, while parameter-efficient methods update a smaller set, such as adapters or low-rank updates. The choice affects training memory, storage, and adaptation capacity. Compare approaches for the target task rather than assuming the smallest update always works.

lessons.title: Prepare suitable data
lessons.body: Training examples should reflect the intended task and respect the applicable data permissions. Split data to prevent related examples or future information from leaking into evaluation. Review label or demonstration quality and include relevant input types. A small or biased fine-tuning set can shift model behavior in undesirable ways.

lessons.title: Compare update methods
lessons.body: A frozen-base method can train added parameters while keeping original weights fixed, reducing the number of trainable parameters. This can reduce optimizer-state memory, but it does not eliminate the cost of the base model or guarantee lower inference latency. Full fine-tuning can offer more flexibility at greater training cost. Measure the actual implementation on the target hardware.

lessons.title: Check retained behavior
lessons.body: Adaptation can improve the target task while degrading capabilities the pretrained model previously handled. Evaluate both target performance and retained behaviors that matter to the application, including safety or formatting requirements. Compare with the original model and relevant baselines on held-out cases. Investigate regressions rather than relying only on training loss.

lessons.title: Version the release
lessons.body: Record the base model, tokenizer, training data version, configuration, and adapter or full-weight artifact. Ensure the serving stack loads the intended combination, and test it under realistic inputs. If an adapter is deployed separately, its compatibility with the base version matters. Keep a rollback path and monitor behavior after release.

topics.title: Loss balancing
topics.description: Relative loss weights determine each objective's influence; inspect task-specific progress to catch domination or collapse.

lessons.title: Combine objectives explicitly
lessons.body: A shared model with two tasks can optimize L = a*L1 + b*L2. The weights a and b determine how each objective contributes to the shared parameter gradient. Their effects depend on loss reduction, units, and gradient magnitudes, not just the numerical values of the weights.

lessons.title: Inspect scale and reduction
lessons.body: If a token loss is summed over 100 positions while a classification loss is averaged over examples, sequence length changes their relative emphasis. Define both reductions before choosing weights. Similar scalar loss values can still produce very different gradients in shared layers.

lessons.title: Notice conflicting gradients
lessons.body: Two tasks can prefer opposite updates to shared parameters. Track task-specific validation metrics and, when diagnosing interference, compare their gradient norms and directions in shared layers. A falling total loss can conceal a task whose quality is deteriorating.

lessons.title: Tune against task requirements
lessons.body: Compare candidate weight settings with fixed training data and a stated budget. If one task has a minimum acceptable recall, enforce that constraint when choosing among trade-offs rather than minimizing only the weighted loss. Include separate single-task models to detect whether sharing hurts either objective.

topics.title: Gradient clipping
topics.description: Clipping bounds gradient magnitude to limit unstable updates but should not conceal persistently exploding gradients.

lessons.title: Bound the global gradient norm
lessons.body: Global norm clipping rescales the combined gradient vector when its norm exceeds a threshold. For norm n and threshold c, multiply gradients by min(1, c/n) when n is nonzero. This preserves the direction of the combined gradient while limiting its magnitude.

lessons.title: Calculate a clipped update
lessons.body: For gradients [3, 4], the Euclidean norm is 5. With a clipping threshold of 2, the scale is 2/5, giving [1.2, 1.6]. Clipping each value independently would give a different direction, so value clipping and global norm clipping are not interchangeable.

lessons.title: Place clipping at the update boundary
lessons.body: Clip after the backward pass has produced the gradients for an optimizer step. With gradient accumulation, that normally means after all contributing microbatches. With scaled mixed-precision gradients, unscale before clipping so the threshold applies to the actual gradient rather than an arbitrary loss-scaling factor.

lessons.title: Monitor how often clipping happens
lessons.body: Log the pre-clipping norm and the fraction of updates clipped. Frequent extreme norms can indicate an excessive learning rate, unstable recurrence, or problematic examples. Clipping is not a repair for NaN gradients, and adaptive optimizers can transform a clipped gradient into an update with a different scale.

topics.title: Mixed precision
topics.description: Lower precision can reduce memory and accelerate training, while sensitive operations may require higher precision or loss scaling.

lessons.title: Use precision selectively
lessons.body: Mixed-precision training runs suitable operations in lower precision while retaining higher precision where needed. FP16 and BF16 use fewer bits than FP32 but have different exponent ranges and precision. Hardware support and kernel choice determine whether the change actually improves speed.

lessons.title: Understand loss scaling
lessons.body: Small FP16 gradients can underflow to zero. Loss scaling multiplies the loss before backpropagation and divides the resulting gradients by the same scale before updating parameters. Dynamic scaling reduces the scale after detected overflow and skips invalid updates; BF16 generally needs scaling less often because of its wider exponent range.

lessons.title: Protect sensitive calculations
lessons.body: Large reductions, normalization statistics, and operations such as exponentials may need higher-precision accumulation or stable implementations. Use the framework's supported automatic casting rules before manually converting every tensor. Keep clipping after gradient unscaling and check that skipped steps do not incorrectly advance the learning-rate schedule.

lessons.title: Compare with an FP32 reference
lessons.body: Measure peak training memory, step time after warmup, and held-out quality against a comparable FP32 run. Inspect non-finite losses and gradient statistics rather than checking speed alone. Lower-precision activations do not imply that parameters, optimizer state, and all temporary buffers use half the memory.

topics.title: Checkpointing and recovery
topics.description: A resumable checkpoint includes model and optimizer state and often scheduler and random state, not just weights.

lessons.title: Save a resumable state
lessons.body: Model weights allow prediction, but resuming training also needs optimizer state, the current step, and any learning-rate scheduler state. Mixed-precision training may need gradient-scaler state. Record the model configuration and data version so the stored tensors can be interpreted correctly.

lessons.title: Preserve the data position
lessons.body: For a close continuation, save random-generator states and the sampler or data-loader position when supported. Restarting at the beginning of an epoch repeats examples if the checkpoint was taken midway through it. Distributed workers may each have relevant random state and data progress.

lessons.title: Publish only complete checkpoints
lessons.body: Write a new checkpoint to a temporary location and mark or rename it as complete only after all required files are durable. Keep an older verified checkpoint until the new one can be loaded. A partially written distributed shard set must not be advertised as a recoverable training state.

lessons.title: Rehearse a restart
lessons.body: Run several steps, save, reload in a fresh process, and verify the restored step, learning rate, and optimizer buffers. Compare the next loss and update with an uninterrupted reference under controlled randomness. Exact equality may be unavailable with nondeterministic kernels, so state the tolerance and recovery guarantee.

topics.title: Representation probing
topics.description: A probe tests whether information is recoverable from hidden states but does not prove the model causally uses it.

lessons.title: Ask what a hidden state contains
lessons.body: A probe is a model trained to predict a property from a network's hidden representations. Freeze the original network and collect representations from a chosen layer. A successful probe shows that its training procedure can recover information from those representations, not that the original model uses it.

lessons.title: Control the probe's capacity
lessons.body: A linear probe can test whether a property is accessible through a simple linear mapping. A larger nonlinear probe may learn a difficult mapping itself. Compare probe capacity and sample size, and include controls such as shuffled labels to detect memorization or an overly easy evaluation setup.

lessons.title: Keep probing splits independent
lessons.body: Separate probe-training examples from probe-evaluation examples and group related records when needed. Choosing the best layer on the same examples used for final reporting inflates the result. A feature that reveals the label through collection artifacts can make a probe look informative for the wrong reason.

lessons.title: Distinguish decoding from causal use
lessons.body: If a sentiment probe succeeds, the original classifier may still rely on a different signal. Carefully designed interventions or ablations can test whether changing that information changes the model's output. Such interventions can also move representations off distribution, so their results need separate controls.

topics.title: Neural calibration
topics.description: Neural classifiers can be confidently wrong, so assess calibration separately from accuracy and ranking.

lessons.title: Compare confidence with correctness
lessons.body: A classifier is calibrated when predictions assigned a given confidence are correct about that fraction of the time on the population evaluated. If 100 predictions near 0.8 confidence contain only 60 correct answers, that group is overconfident. Accuracy alone does not expose this mismatch.

lessons.title: Build a reliability view
lessons.body: Group predictions into confidence bins and compare each bin's average confidence with observed accuracy. Include counts: sparse bins have substantial uncertainty. Expected calibration error summarizes bin gaps but depends on binning; inspect reliability plots alongside proper scoring rules such as negative log-likelihood or the Brier score.

lessons.title: Fit temperature on held-out logits
lessons.body: Temperature scaling divides logits by a fitted positive scalar before softmax. Fit the temperature on a calibration partition separate from model training and final testing. A single positive temperature preserves the largest logit's class while changing confidence, so it can improve calibration without changing top-class accuracy.

lessons.title: Recheck the deployment population
lessons.body: Calibration can deteriorate when class prevalence or input conditions change. Measure relevant subgroups as well as overall behavior before using probabilities in cost-sensitive decisions. A calibrated score does not by itself specify when to act or guarantee that a rare, high-cost error is acceptable.

topics.title: Robustness testing
topics.description: Robustness evaluation uses plausible corruptions and distribution changes rather than relying on clean benchmark accuracy alone.

lessons.title: Define plausible changes
lessons.body: Robustness testing measures behavior when inputs differ from clean training examples. For an image service, useful changes may include blur, dim lighting, or a new camera. Choose perturbations from expected deployment conditions rather than assuming that any synthetic noise represents a realistic failure.

lessons.title: Measure degradation by severity
lessons.body: Evaluate the same held-out examples at several blur strengths and report performance for each strength alongside the clean result. Preserve labels only where the transformed example still supports them. A transformation that makes the object unrecognizable tests a different limit from a mild camera defect.

lessons.title: Test combinations and slices
lessons.body: Low light and motion blur may occur together even if each was tested separately. Break down errors by relevant groups such as object size or device type, and include sample counts. One aggregate corruption score can conceal a severe failure in a common operating condition.

lessons.title: Keep a held-out robustness suite
lessons.body: Use development corruptions to guide improvements, then evaluate on separate examples and conditions that did not drive tuning. Compare clean quality too: robustness changes can trade off other requirements. Define how the service detects or handles unsupported inputs when the model cannot meet the required quality.

topics.title: Ablation studies
topics.description: Controlled ablations estimate a component's contribution when training data, compute, and evaluation are held comparable.

lessons.title: Ask a component-level question
lessons.body: An ablation compares a full system with a version where one component is removed or changed. For example, compare a residual network with a compatible no-skip variant to ask whether skip connections help under the chosen setup. State the hypothesis before looking at results.

lessons.title: Hold the comparison conditions steady
lessons.body: Use the same data partitions, evaluation code, and stated training budget for both variants. Removing a component can also change parameter count or compute, so report those differences. Decide whether each variant receives equal tuning effort or whether a fixed recipe is intentionally being tested.

lessons.title: Repeat and inspect interactions
lessons.body: A small gain from one random seed may disappear across repeated runs. Report variation and compare paired seeds when practical. If removing component A hurts only when component B is present, their interaction matters; a single remove-one-component table cannot fully describe that relationship.

lessons.title: Limit the conclusion
lessons.body: If a component improves the tested metric, conclude that it helped under the measured data and training conditions. Do not infer that it is necessary for every task or that the proposed mechanism is proven. Distinguish an inference-time removal from retraining without the component, since they answer different questions.

topics.title: Scaling laws and compute
topics.description: Scaling laws are empirical trends, not guarantees; data quality, task relevance, and inference cost constrain useful scaling.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Scaling laws summarize empirical relationships between measures such as model size, training data, compute, and loss within a particular training setup. They help plan experiments, but a curve fitted to one setting does not guarantee performance on a different architecture, dataset, or task.

lessons.title: Separate compute budgets
lessons.body: Training compute covers optimization and data processing; inference compute recurs when the deployed model serves requests. A larger model can have acceptable training cost but exceed latency or serving budgets. Estimate both budgets using expected traffic and measured performance.

lessons.title: Consider data quality
lessons.body: More examples are useful only in the context of their quality, diversity, relevance, and licensing constraints. Duplicates or evaluation contamination can distort apparent gains. Track data provenance and evaluate on representative, appropriately held-out examples.

lessons.title: Fit and test the trend
lessons.body: Measure comparable runs at multiple scales and fit a trend only over a range with sufficient evidence. Report uncertainty and check whether an extrapolation changes the architecture or data regime. Compare predicted improvements with the cost of the next experiment.

lessons.title: Choose for the application
lessons.body: Compare candidate models on the task's quality metrics, failure modes, latency, memory, and cost. A lower aggregate language-model loss need not translate to acceptable performance in every downstream use. Prefer the smallest solution that meets the measured requirements rather than assuming bigger is always better.

topics.title: Distributed data parallelism
topics.description: Data-parallel replicas synchronize gradients, and communication overhead can limit throughput as workers are added.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Data parallelism keeps a model replica on each worker and processes different portions of a batch in parallel. Workers synchronize gradients before the optimizer update so their replicas remain consistent under the intended training setup.

lessons.title: Synchronize gradients
lessons.body: Each worker computes gradients for its local examples. A collective operation such as all-reduce aggregates gradients across workers; implementations often average them. The exact scaling must match the loss reduction and local batch sizes, especially when batches differ.

lessons.title: Account for effective batch
lessons.body: With four workers processing eight examples each and no gradient accumulation, the global batch contains 32 examples per synchronized update. Gradient accumulation can increase that effective batch. Changing batch size may require retuning learning rate or other settings.

lessons.title: Measure scaling limits
lessons.body: Adding workers can improve throughput, but communication, data loading, and synchronization delays can limit gains. Measure examples per second, accelerator utilization, and time spent communicating rather than assuming linear speedup.

lessons.title: Validate and recover
lessons.body: Check that data sharding avoids unintended duplication and that distributed metrics use correct aggregation. Save model, optimizer, scheduler, and relevant training state for recovery. Compare held-out behavior with a baseline because a faster run is not necessarily an equivalent model.

topics.title: Tensor and pipeline parallelism
topics.description: Tensor parallelism partitions operations and pipeline parallelism partitions layers; both introduce communication and scheduling trade-offs.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Model parallelism distributes parts of a model across devices. Tensor parallelism splits work within operations, while pipeline parallelism assigns different layers or stages to different devices.

lessons.title: Partition an operation
lessons.body: Tensor parallelism can partition a large matrix operation across devices and combine or exchange intermediate results as required. It can help a model fit or use multiple devices, but frequent communication makes network performance important.

lessons.title: Partition stages
lessons.body: Pipeline parallelism places consecutive model stages on different devices. Activations move forward between stages and gradients move backward during training. Microbatches can keep stages busy, though scheduling introduces idle periods and memory trade-offs.

lessons.title: Measure the bottleneck
lessons.body: Compare throughput, device memory, communication time, and stage utilization. An uneven pipeline stage can slow the rest, while tensor parallelism can be limited by collective communication. More devices do not automatically improve throughput.

lessons.title: Validate equivalence
