lessons.body: Test tensor shapes, synchronization, and output or gradient behavior against a small reference setup. Record partitioning and checkpoint state so training can be resumed consistently. Numerical differences can arise from operation ordering and hardware.

topics.title: Activation checkpointing
topics.description: Checkpointing recomputes selected activations during backpropagation to exchange extra compute for lower memory use.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Activation checkpointing reduces training memory by retaining selected intermediate values and recomputing others during the backward pass. It trades additional computation for lower activation storage.

lessons.title: Follow the passes
lessons.body: During the forward pass, a checkpointed region keeps only the values needed to rerun it. During backpropagation, the region is recomputed so its intermediate activations are available for gradient calculation.

lessons.title: Choose boundaries
lessons.body: Checkpointing more regions can save activation memory but add more recomputation overhead. Measure peak memory and step time for representative batches. The best boundaries depend on the model, framework, and available hardware.

lessons.title: Handle state and randomness
lessons.body: Recomputation must be compatible with operations that use randomness or mutate state. Follow the framework's checkpointing rules for random state and side effects. An operation that behaves differently when rerun can produce incorrect gradients.

lessons.title: Validate the change
lessons.body: Compare outputs and gradients against a non-checkpointed reference on a small case within suitable numerical tolerances. Measure training speed and peak memory, and distinguish activation checkpointing from saving model checkpoints for recovery.

topics.title: Quantization-aware training
topics.description: Quantization-aware training simulates low-precision effects during training to reduce quality loss after conversion.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Quantization-aware training simulates selected low-precision effects during training. It aims to help a model adapt before conversion to a quantized representation for an intended deployment target.

lessons.title: Simulate quantization
lessons.body: A typical workflow inserts fake-quantization operations that approximate rounding and clipping while training retains suitable higher-precision state. The exact operators and supported formats depend on the framework and target hardware.

lessons.title: Choose a target
lessons.body: Define the deployment backend, supported operations, precision, and performance constraints before preparing the model. A quantization scheme unsupported by the target cannot be assumed to provide the expected speed or memory savings.

lessons.title: Train and convert
lessons.body: Fine-tune or train with the simulated quantization behavior, then convert using the framework's supported procedure. Preserve preprocessing and version information. Conversion can change numerical behavior, so evaluate the converted artifact itself.

lessons.title: Measure the outcome
lessons.body: Compare held-out quality, model size, latency, and resource use with a suitable baseline on representative hardware. Investigate quality regressions and unsupported operations. Quantization-aware training does not guarantee no accuracy loss.

topics.title: Knowledge distillation
topics.description: Distillation trains a smaller student using teacher outputs or intermediate signals and must be judged on task outcomes.

lessons.title: Transfer from teacher to student
lessons.body: Knowledge distillation trains a student model using information from a teacher, often to reduce inference cost or latency. The student can learn from the teacher's output probabilities, logits, generated examples, or intermediate representations. A smaller model is not automatically better: compare task quality, resource use, and operational constraints against both teacher and baseline.

lessons.title: Learn from soft targets
lessons.body: In classification, a teacher's probability distribution can convey relative preference among classes, not just its top choice. A student can minimize a divergence from that distribution, sometimes alongside ordinary loss against labeled targets. Temperature rescales logits before softmax and can reveal differences among lower-probability classes. The exact objective and any temperature-dependent scaling must be defined consistently in the implementation.

lessons.title: Combine objectives carefully
lessons.body: A common objective combines a supervised loss on available labels with a distillation loss from the teacher. Their relative weights change the gradients the student receives. A teacher's confident mistake can be copied, so validate the weights on data that reflects the intended task. Record the teacher version, training data, temperature, and loss definition to make results reproducible.

lessons.title: Select transfer data
lessons.body: The examples used to obtain teacher targets shape what the student can learn. Include relevant input types and hard cases, and check data permissions and label quality. If the student sees a narrow distribution, it may match the teacher there but fail elsewhere. Keep evaluation examples separate from transfer-data selection and tuning.

lessons.title: Evaluate the deployed student
lessons.body: Compare the student with the teacher and an appropriate non-distilled baseline on held-out task metrics, important slices, and failure cases. Measure latency, memory, throughput, and cost on the target hardware under realistic input sizes. A low teacher-matching loss does not prove that the student meets the application's quality requirements. Monitor the deployed model if the data or environment changes.

topics.title: Pruning and sparsity
topics.description: Removing weights reduces parameter count, but speed gains depend on sparse kernels and target hardware.

lessons.title: Distinguish sparse patterns
lessons.body: Unstructured pruning removes individual weights, often according to magnitude. Structured pruning removes groups such as channels or attention heads. Both reduce active connections, but their storage and execution consequences differ: a dense tensor containing zeros still occupies dense storage unless its representation changes.

lessons.title: Prune and recover quality
lessons.body: Start from a trained reference, remove a stated fraction of weights or groups, then fine-tune if the procedure allows it. Measure the immediate quality drop and the quality after recovery separately. Record recovery compute so a compressed model is not presented as free to produce.

lessons.title: Match sparsity to the runtime
lessons.body: Irregular zeros may not accelerate a dense matrix kernel. Some hardware supports particular block or N:M sparsity patterns; structured channel removal can instead produce smaller dense operations. Benchmark the exported representation on the actual runtime before claiming a speed or memory benefit.

lessons.title: Report the full trade-off
lessons.body: Compare artifact size, peak memory, latency at the intended batch size, and held-out quality with the unpruned model. Include subgroup regressions and any change to model shapes. A 50% reduction in nonzero weights is not equivalent to a 50% reduction in end-to-end inference time.

topics.title: Architecture search
topics.description: Architecture search explores a bounded design space and can overfit validation results or consume excessive compute.

lessons.title: Define a bounded search space
lessons.body: Architecture search selects among design choices such as layer width, depth, and operator type. Specify legal candidates and resource limits before launching trials. A search space already encodes assumptions: excluding a family of models prevents the search from discovering it, regardless of the optimizer.

lessons.title: Use proxies carefully
lessons.body: Short training runs or reduced-resolution inputs can cheaply rank candidates, but their rankings may differ from full-budget results. Retrain promising architectures under the final recipe. If candidates share weights in a supernetwork, inherited-weight performance is a proxy rather than a standalone evaluation.

lessons.title: Separate search from final assessment
lessons.body: Thousands of candidate evaluations can adapt the search to validation noise. Keep a final held-out test outside architecture selection and report multiple independent retrainings when feasible. Charge failed trials and proxy evaluations to the total search budget, not only the cost of training the winner.

lessons.title: Search for a deployable trade-off
lessons.body: Treat quality and measured latency or memory as separate objectives or constraints. A candidate with fewer arithmetic operations may be slower because of unsupported operators or memory traffic. Retain the Pareto frontier: candidates for which no measured alternative is at least as good on every objective and better on one.

topics.title: Continual learning
topics.description: Continual learning adapts to new tasks while measuring and mitigating loss of previously acquired capabilities.

lessons.title: Measure forgetting after an update
lessons.body: Continual learning updates a model as tasks or data distributions arrive over time. Training on new data can overwrite capabilities useful for older tasks, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. Evaluate earlier tasks after each update rather than reporting only the latest task's quality.

lessons.title: Compare retention strategies
lessons.body: Replay mixes selected old examples with new training data. Regularization can discourage changes to parameters judged important for previous tasks, while adapters can isolate some task-specific changes. These methods have different storage and compute costs, and replay must respect data retention permissions.

lessons.title: Track an evaluation matrix
lessons.body: Make one row per training stage and one column per evaluation task. If task A falls from 90% after stage A to 75% after stage B, its measured accuracy dropped by 15 percentage points. The matrix also shows whether later learning improves earlier tasks rather than only causing forgetting.

lessons.title: State the task-information assumption
lessons.body: Some systems know the task identity at inference and select a matching head; others must distinguish all classes without that information. These settings are not directly comparable. Preserve chronological evaluation and include a frozen reference to distinguish adaptation gains from regressions in older capabilities.

topics.title: Adversarial robustness
topics.description: Robustness claims are relative to a defined threat model; no single attack suite covers every manipulation.

lessons.title: Specify a threat model
lessons.body: An adversarial robustness claim must state what an adversary can observe and change. For an image classifier, a bounded pixel perturbation is different from a physical change to lighting or viewpoint. Define the allowed set, model access, and success criterion before interpreting a robustness score.

lessons.title: Evaluate adaptive attacks
lessons.body: On an authorized test model, use attacks that account for the actual preprocessing and defense rather than attacking an unrelated surrogate alone. Evaluate several attack settings and budgets within the stated threat model. Report clean accuracy as well as the fraction of examples correctly classified under the evaluated attacks.

lessons.title: Look for misleading gradients
lessons.body: A defense can make gradients uninformative without making decisions robust. Unexpectedly stronger black-box than white-box results, or attack success that fails to improve with a larger search budget, merit investigation. A failed attack supplies an empirical test result, not a proof that no allowed attack exists.

lessons.title: Separate empirical and certified claims
lessons.body: Adversarial training can improve performance against the perturbations represented during training but need not protect against other manipulations. A robustness certificate applies only under its mathematical assumptions and stated radius. Report those limits and evaluate ordinary distribution shifts separately from adversarial perturbations.

topics.title: Model privacy attacks
topics.description: Membership inference and extraction tests probe information exposure but do not alone establish a privacy guarantee.

lessons.title: Separate privacy questions
lessons.body: Membership inference asks whether a record was part of training. Model extraction aims to reproduce model behavior, while training-data extraction seeks memorized examples. These are different risks. Define the protected information and the access available to an authorized evaluator before selecting a privacy test.

lessons.title: Construct a matched audit
lessons.body: For a membership audit, compare known members with nonmembers drawn from a comparable population. Otherwise, an apparent attack may merely detect a distribution difference. Use authorized or synthetic data, separate attack development from evaluation, and report false-positive rates alongside detection rates.

lessons.title: Reduce exposure deliberately
lessons.body: Restrict unnecessary output detail and query access, and apply data minimization before training. Differentially private training can bound the influence of a protected unit under a stated privacy definition and budget. State whether that unit is a record or a person, since several records may belong to one person.

lessons.title: Interpret negative results narrowly
lessons.body: An unsuccessful audit does not establish that the model never memorizes or exposes sensitive data. The conclusion depends on the attack family, sample size, and access tested. Record those limits, protect any recovered test examples, and use formal guarantees only when their assumptions and accounting actually apply.

topics.title: Deep-model uncertainty
topics.description: Ensembles and approximate Bayesian methods estimate some uncertainty but can remain overconfident under distribution shift.

lessons.title: Distinguish sources of uncertainty
lessons.body: Aleatoric uncertainty reflects ambiguity or noise in observations under the chosen task. Epistemic uncertainty reflects uncertainty about the learned model and can sometimes shrink with informative data. This distinction depends on the modeling assumptions; one softmax confidence score does not identify both sources.

lessons.title: Compare multiple predictions
lessons.body: A deep ensemble trains several models and compares their predictions. Stochastic methods such as Monte Carlo dropout sample predictions from one model under a particular approximation. Agreement is useful evidence but can be misleading when all members share the same training gaps or architectural biases.

lessons.title: Evaluate intervals or abstention
lessons.body: For regression intervals, measure coverage together with interval width: an interval that always spans every plausible value is uninformative despite high coverage. For selective classification, report error as a function of the fraction of predictions retained. Choose abstention thresholds on validation data rather than the final test.

lessons.title: Challenge uncertainty under shift
lessons.body: Evaluate known distribution changes and examples outside the supported operating range. A model or ensemble can confidently agree on an incorrect answer far from its training data. If using conformal intervals, state the exchangeability assumptions behind their coverage guarantee instead of assuming it survives arbitrary shifts.

topics.title: Graph neural networks
topics.description: Message-passing graph networks aggregate neighborhood information and can oversmooth or leak structure across data splits.

lessons.title: Aggregate a neighborhood
lessons.body: A message-passing layer computes messages from neighboring nodes and combines them with a node's current representation. The aggregation must respect the graph's ordering invariance, often through a sum or mean. After several layers, a node can receive information from nodes multiple edges away.

lessons.title: Calculate a simple message
lessons.body: If a node's neighbors have scalar features 2 and 4, mean aggregation returns 3. A learned update can combine that value with the node's own feature. Specify self-loops and directed-edge handling: including the node itself or reversing edges changes which information reaches it.

lessons.title: Recognize depth and sampling limits
lessons.body: Repeated averaging can make nearby node representations difficult to distinguish, an effect called oversmoothing. Compressing a rapidly growing neighborhood into a fixed-size vector can also lose information. Neighbor sampling limits computation but changes the messages observed, so evaluate its effect rather than treating it as exact full-graph computation.

lessons.title: Align graph visibility with deployment
lessons.body: For future-link prediction, build message-passing edges only from information available before the prediction cutoff. State whether test nodes are visible during training or entirely new at evaluation. Compare with a model using node features alone to measure the benefit of graph structure under that protocol.

topics.title: Multimodal fusion
topics.description: Early, late, and cross-attention fusion differ in interaction depth and behavior when a modality is missing.

lessons.title: Choose where modalities interact
lessons.body: Early fusion combines modality features before much shared processing. Late fusion combines predictions from separate models. Cross-attention lets representations from one modality select information from another. These choices differ in interaction capacity, training requirements, and whether individual modality encoders can be run independently.

lessons.title: Align paired observations
lessons.body: For video and audio, verify that time windows refer to the same event. For image-text training, inspect whether captions describe the paired image. Misalignment can teach false associations; a model may minimize loss through dataset shortcuts without learning the cross-modal relationship the task requires.

lessons.title: Plan for a missing modality
lessons.body: A deployed system may receive an image without a caption or audio with a failed sensor stream. Evaluate those cases explicitly. Modality dropout during training can support a defined fallback, but substituting zeros at inference is not automatically valid if the model never learned that convention.

lessons.title: Verify that fusion adds evidence
lessons.body: Compare the fused model with each unimodal model on the same split, then inspect examples with contradictory inputs. If removing one modality leaves performance unchanged, the other may dominate. Report quality and latency for each availability pattern rather than only the fully paired benchmark.

topics.title: Inference optimization
topics.description: Batching, caching, kernel fusion, and sequence length affect throughput, memory, and tail latency differently.

lessons.title: Profile the serving workload
lessons.body: Define input sizes, arrival rate, concurrency, and the latency percentile the service must meet. Measure preprocessing, model execution, and output handling after warmup on target hardware. A fast isolated forward pass can still produce poor end-to-end latency if requests queue or data transfer dominates.

lessons.title: Trade batching against waiting
lessons.body: Combining requests into a batch can improve device utilization and throughput, but waiting to form the batch increases latency. Dynamic batching needs a maximum wait and size appropriate to the workload. Benchmark bursty arrivals and long inputs, not only a continuous stream of equal-sized requests.

lessons.title: Reduce repeated computation
lessons.body: Autoregressive decoders can cache attention keys and values from previous tokens instead of recomputing them at each step. The cache grows with sequence length and concurrent requests, consuming memory. Kernel fusion can reduce intermediate memory traffic, but support depends on the exported graph, precision, and runtime.

lessons.title: Verify quality and tail latency
lessons.body: After changing precision, compilation, or kernels, compare outputs within task-appropriate tolerances and rerun held-out quality checks. Report peak memory, throughput, and tail latency under realistic load. An optimization that improves average speed but causes out-of-memory failures on long requests is not a successful serving change.
